phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], fully voiced in Old Norse initial position, as in English 'bow'.
The falling diphthong [ɑu] — open back vowel gliding to rounded u, like the 'ow' of English 'cow'; the Old Norse diphthong that later Icelandic monophthongized.
Voiced velar fricative [ɣ] between vowels — not a hard stop: Old Norse g softens medially to a breathy glide, here palatalized before i toward something close to English 'y'.
Short high front [i], unstressed final syllable, as in the last beat of 'happy'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BOW-yee' — the first syllable rhymes with English 'cow', and the medial g is not a stop but a soft voiced glide between the vowels, so the second syllable lands almost like 'yee'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Baugi, the jötunn brother of Suttungr, named in Skáldskaparmál and listed among the giants in the þulur.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ — the Viking-Age runic rendering, transliterated b-au-k-i; the k-rune writes the g, and no rune marks the medial fricative the manuscripts spell with g.

kin.label: Word-kin
kin.form: baugr, the Old Norse masculine noun 'ring, circlet' — the word to which the name is usually, though not securely, connected; it also stands in baugeiðr, 'ring-oath', the very oath Hávamál accuses Óðinn of breaking in this story.

pronunciation.note: Baugi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The tier reports the name's orthography, not the figure's standing; the corpus names him in one story and one list, and both are written in unbroken Latin letters.

domains.title: Giant, Brother of Suttungr
domains.subtitle: The Keeper of the Door at Hnitbjǫrg
domains.lead: Baugi is the giant who holds the one door that matters in the story of the mead of poetry: brother to Suttungr, who hoards the mead inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and master of the nine thralls whose deaths open the way to Óðinn's bargain. He is the hinge of the whole theft — the labour-contractor, the reluctant accomplice, and the would-be cheat whose auger-stroke misses a snake by an inch.

cards.name: Hnitbjǫrg
cards.desc: The mountain — its name plausibly 'the clashing rocks' — inside which Suttungr shut the mead of poetry, with his daughter Gunnlǫð set to guard it. Baugi's auger makes the only door it ever had.

cards.name: Rati
cards.desc: The auger Óðinn puts in Baugi's hands — 'the traveller', from the verb rata. Baugi bores the tunnel with it, and nearly ends the story with one stroke of it.

cards.name: The Whetstone
cards.desc: The sharpening stone Óðinn tosses among Baugi's nine mowing thralls; in scrambling to claim it they cut each other's throats, and Baugi is left with a harvest and no hands.

cards.name: The Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: Kvasir's blood brewed with honey, held in Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són — the drink that makes a poet or a sage of whoever tastes it, and the prize the whole bargain is for.

symbols.name: Hnitbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: The mountain of the mead — hoard and fortress in one, opened by craft rather than force

symbols.name: Rati
symbols.meaning: The auger that gnaws through stone — the tool that makes the door, and nearly the weapon that closes the story

symbols.name: The whetstone
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's thrown bait — the small object whose coveting empties Baugi's fields of nine workers at a stroke

symbols.name: The nine thralls' scythes
symbols.meaning: The harvest-tools honed too well — honest labour's edge turned into mutual death by one act of sharpening

symbols.name: Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són
symbols.meaning: The three vessels of the mead — 'heart-stirrer', 'vessel', and 'reconciliation' — emptied in three draughts

mythology.lead: Baugi's entire mythology is one episode, and it is the most consequential single episode in the mythology of poetry: the mead heist of Skáldskaparmál. He appears only there and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door, and never again. But that once is the door through which all skaldic poetry claims to have come.

myths.title: The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg
myths.text:
The story begins before Baugi enters it. From the peace-making of Æsir and Vanir is made Kvasir, wisest of beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar kill him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes a poet or a scholar of whoever drinks it, keeping it in three vessels — Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són. The dwarfs then drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his wife with a millstone, and Gilling's son Suttungr takes revenge: he sets the dwarfs on a tide-washed skerry, and they buy their lives with the mead. Suttungr carries it home, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it.

Only now does Snorri bring Baugi on stage, in a single sentence of genealogy: Suttungr had a brother, and his name was Baugi. The hoard is sealed, the guard is set, and the god who wants the mead does not go to its owner — he goes to the owner's brother.

myths.title: The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls
myths.text:
Óðinn comes walking to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-doer' — a name that is not a disguise so much as an announcement. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay. Bǫlverkr offers to sharpen their scythes, and the whetstone he pulls from his cloak hones so well that all nine want to buy it. He says it will be sold dearly, and throws it up among them; in the scramble to catch it, each thrall swings his scythe at another's neck, and all nine lie dead in the field.

That evening Bǫlverkr lodges with Baugi, and Baugi pours out his troubles: his nine thralls are dead and the hay harvest stands uncut. The god has engineered the vacancy he is about to fill — the labour shortage is the lock, and he made it himself.

myths.title: Nine Men's Work for One Draught
myths.text:
Bǫlverkr makes the offer: he will do the work of nine men through the summer, and his wage is one drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi is careful here, and Snorri gives him the one honest line in the story: he answers that the mead is not his to give — Suttungr alone has control of it — but he will go with Bǫlverkr and they will try together whether they can get it. The bargain is struck: a summer's labour against a hope, with Baugi as broker.

Bǫlverkr does the work of nine all summer. When winter comes they go to Suttungr and Baugi puts the case — and Suttungr refuses flatly: not one drop of the mead. Baugi's brokerage has failed on its stated terms; what remains is the attempt he half-promised, the trying of stratagems.

myths.title: Rati and the Two Blowings
myths.text:
Bǫlverkr now asks Baugi for other ways in, and produces the auger called Rati. Baugi bores into the mountain, and says the hole is through. Bǫlverkr leans down and blows into the bore — and the stone-chips fly back into his face. He knows then, Snorri says, that Baugi meant to betray him: the hole is blind. Baugi bores again, and this time when Bǫlverkr blows, the chips fly inward and away. The tunnel is through.

Bǫlverkr turns himself into a snake and crawls into the hole — and Baugi strikes after him with the auger, and misses. It is the story's tightest instant: the accomplice becomes the assassin at the threshold, and the mead of all poetry hangs on one failed stroke. Inside waits Gunnlǫð; Óðinn lies with her three nights, wins leave for three draughts, and empties Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són entire. Then he rises as an eagle with all the mead in him, Suttungr in eagle-shape hard behind, and the Æsir set out their vats in Ásgarðr's court — Baugi's door standing open in the mountain behind them all.

myths.title: Óðinn's Own Version
myths.text:
Hávamál lets Óðinn boast of the same theft in his own voice, and the differences are instructive. The god names Rati — 'Rati's mouth I made room for me, and it gnawed the rock' — names Gunnlǫð and the golden seat, names Óðrœrir come up among the Æsir. He names Suttungr defrauded of his mead and Gunnlǫð left weeping, and he names the instrument of it: the baugeiðr, the ring-oath Óðinn swore and broke — 'who can trust him?'

But Hávamál never names Baugi. In the god's own telling, the brother at the door has already vanished — the contract, the auger, the missed stroke, all absorbed into Óðinn's solitary cunning. Snorri's prose preserves what the god's boasting omits: that the door had a keeper, that the keeper had a price, and that the keeper tried, at the last moment, to close it on the snake.

lore.syncretism: Baugi himself has no cross-border reflex — no Old English or continental cognate figure, no cult, no charm; he is a person the Icelandic tradition made for one narrative. The myth he serves, however, sits in one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European study: the theft of the divine intoxicant. The standard parallel is Vedic — the śyena, the eagle or falcon who snatches the soma and brings it to the gods (Rigveda 4.26–27) — set beside Óðinn in eagle-shape carrying off the mead in his body. The comparison was drawn in the nineteenth century and is still registered, with due caution, in the modern handbooks: Lindow treats the mead myth as the northern member of a genuine inheritance while warning against flattening its specifically Norse machinery — the labour contract, the auger, the broken oath. Baugi's own role belongs to that northern machinery: the intermediary who can be bought, the door that opens from the inside. His closest structural kin in the corpus are the other giants whose households Óðinn penetrates by guile, above all the world of [[suttungr|Suttungr]] itself and the deep giant-lore of [[ymir|Ymir]]'s kin.
lore.culturalLegacy: Baugi's afterlife is mostly the afterlife of the drink he failed to keep. Skaldic poetry — the entire court-poetry tradition of the Viking and medieval North — called itself by kennings drawn from this myth: Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's theft, Óðrœrir's wave. Every one of those names is a character in the heist except its doorkeeper; the corpus never minted a 'Baugi's mead'. He survives instead as the specialists' hinge-figure: every scholarly treatment of the mead myth, from Finnur Jónsson to Lindow, must reckon with his two functions — the labour-broker who makes the theft logistically possible, and the wavering accomplice whose bore-hole and auger-stroke are the story's closest brush with failure. In modern retellings of the myth he appears under his name in the better handbooks and in the illustrated Eddas of the Norse revival, always in the same posture: halfway through the mountain, one hand on the auger. The mead myth itself has become the North's great parable of inspiration as something stolen, hoarded, and re-stolen — and the god of poetry, [[bragi|Bragi]], pours out what Baugi could not guard.
lore.archaeology: Baugi is an entirely textual figure: no runestone invokes him, no picture stone has been convincingly read as the drilling of Hnitbjǫrg, and no place-name or votive deposit carries his name. His attestation is exactly as wide as his story — Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, preserved principally in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), with the Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis as the other main witnesses, plus his entry in the þulur of giant-names. The mead myth he serves is materially older than its manuscripts: kennings presupposing it — Kvasir's blood, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's booty — are already at work in ninth- and tenth-century skaldic verse, which proves the story's currency centuries before Snorri wrote it down. Hávamál's telling survives in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), the same small codex that carries nearly all the mythological poems. The runic record is silent on the theonym, as on nearly all the jǫtnar.
lore.extendedMeditation: Baugi is the indispensable man nobody remembers. Strip him out and the myth stops cold: without the thralls' deaths there is no vacancy, without the contract there is no access, without the auger in his hand there is no door, and without the door there is no mead — and without the mead, by the tradition's own accounting, there is no poetry at all. Yet he is not a hero of his one story, nor even its villain; he is something rarer in the giant-world of the Eddas, a middleman. He names the limits of his power honestly — the mead is Suttungr's, not mine — and then sells access to what is not his anyway. He helps bore the hole and then tries to kill what crawls through it. The tradition leaves his motives exactly that tangled, and the tangle is the point: every hoard is opened from the inside, by someone whose loyalty is a price rather than a fact. The auger-stroke misses by the width of a snake, and because it misses, poems exist.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Baugi — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᛅᚢᚴᛁ (b-au-k-i, the k-rune ᚴ writing the g and no rune marking the medial fricative the manuscript spelling preserves). Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com address was registered in the ordinary way and is held outside the PuniCodex collection: no form of the name is currently owned, the plain-ASCII domain is watched for release, and this temple claims none.
